cards.title: Growing Uber Eats in underserved regional areas of Australia and New Zealand
cards.headline: Led the strategy workstream for a seven-function program to grow Uber Eats in underserved regional Australia and New Zealand; the country GM approved the plan and regional category position rose about 24 points in a year.
cards.trigger: Growth was uneven, and regional areas lagged metro on restaurant choice and competitive position.
cards.problem: Turn a broad 'grow regional' ambition into a ranked city list with entry rules that five teams could act on, without reducing it to one number, and keep it current as the market changed.

what_i_did.detail: Designed city-prioritisation criteria combining merchant coverage, trip potential and competitive position, then applied them to about 30 priority cities and 34 second-tier cities in Australia, and 12 priority cities in New Zealand.

When Menulog announced its exit in November 2025, widened the plan from 15 to about 30 priority cities to include places where Uber Eats wasn't yet leading, and pushed back on an over-broad New Zealand proposal, narrowing it to 12 cities.
Matched each city tier to specific levers (sales coverage, consumer offers, delivery reliability and speed standards), so each team knew what it owned.
Wrote the fortnightly working-group pack for Acquisition, Consumer, Marketplace, Marketing and Merchant Ops, and built the city-level tracker the group worked from.

cards.artifacts: Prioritisation framework, revised annual plan, project plan, city and area tracker, working-group packs.
cards.outcome: The country GM approved the plan in November 2025 and it became a named growth priority in the 2026 annual plan. Regional Australia category position rose about 24 percentage points year on year, regional trips grew about 50%, active stores in priority areas grew about 35%, and restaurant selection against the nearest competitor went from parity to about 1.35x (program results, shared with Acquisition, Consumer and Marketplace; includes the lift from Menulog's exit). After handover, priority cities kept outgrowing other regional cities on bookings and share (<redacted>).
cards.learning: Explicit entry criteria and staged decisions keep multi-team investment debates grounded when evidence is incomplete. A plan also needs a trigger for re-planning, not just a start date.

cards.title: Preparing for and responding to Menulog's exit from Australia
cards.headline: Wrote the response playbook months before Menulog's exit from Australia and ran governance across six functions; offers launched within 48 hours, and Uber Eats captured the large majority of the share Menulog left.
cards.trigger: A major competitor's exit was possible, and a slow or uncoordinated response would hand its customers and restaurants to others.
cards.problem: Six functions each had their own levers and timelines. The response had to be ready before the announcement, move within days, and be judged on solid evidence afterwards.

what_i_did.detail: Wrote the response playbook months ahead and ran a pre-exit sprint with two drills, so teams knew their offers, owners and triggers in advance.
When Menulog announced its exit in November 2025, coordinated Consumer, Acquisition, Merchant Ops, Marketing, Marketplace and Product so offers went live within 48 hours.
Kept a dated tracker separating our actions from market changes, with written assumptions, so teams worked from one picture instead of competing stories.
Ran a look-back review across the response to separate what drove the gains from what just happened at the same time.

cards.artifacts: Response playbook, drill materials, dated response tracker, summary decks, look-back review.
cards.outcome: Uber Eats captured the large majority of the share Menulog left. Regional Australia category position rose about 11 percentage points in five weeks, and weekly first-time restaurants, customers and couriers rose 30–50% (shared results across six functions).
cards.learning: The response was fast because the decisions were made before the event. A disciplined tracker and an honest look-back turn one-off firefighting into a reusable playbook.

cards.title: Rolling out Uber One price and benefit changes in Japan and Taiwan
cards.headline: Co-wrote the global playbook for Uber One price-and-benefit changes and applied it to the public Japan and Taiwan changes; the full Japan member base moved over on the planned date with no operational incident.
cards.trigger: Uber One prices and benefits changed in Taiwan and then Japan in 2026 (public changes). The region needed a repeatable way to run these changes and to judge whether they worked.
cards.problem: Announcement reactions, new sign-ups and renewals by existing members all happen at different times, so early numbers can look healthy before renewals come due. Each change also involved several product, legal, localisation and web teams, with different customer groups switching on different dates.

what_i_did.detail: Co-wrote the global playbook for membership price changes with two regional colleagues, covering communications timing, ownership, annual-plan treatment, test users and go/no-go checks. Carried the lessons from Taiwan into Japan's readiness checks.

Set measurement rules that kept notices, opt-outs, new sign-ups, active and passive cancellations and renewal-based retention separate, measured annual plans on their own, and labelled cohorts whose renewals hadn't happened yet as 'not yet due', not as lost.

what_i_did.summary: Run the page like a launch
what_i_did.detail: Owned the Japan public Uber One page update: mapped the review chain (product, legal, localisation, web operations), the cutover timing and the pre-publish checks, and kept 'configured' separate from 'seen working in production'.
Wrote the regional impact memo (13 findings across acquisition, opt-outs, churn, engagement and economics), proposed a price-setting framework for the next markets, and briefed regional leadership.

cards.artifacts: Global price-change playbook, regional impact memo, measurement definitions, public-page review map and launch checklists.
cards.outcome: The full Japan member base moved to the new price on the planned date with no operational incident, and Japan's pre-launch tests, built from the playbook, caught a plan defect before customers saw it. Detailed retention and economics results: <redacted>.
cards.learning: Measure customers at the point they actually renew, and treat a price change as a launch with named owners, live evidence and a rollback plan. Announcement-week numbers aren't a retention result.

cards.title: Diagnosing growth by city, category and brand
cards.headline: Led city and category share deep dives for Uber Eats ANZ, including a Sydney diagnosis that moved the team from broad promotions to targeted offers for new, infrequent and lapsed customers.
cards.trigger: Growth was uneven across cities, categories and brands, and market averages couldn't explain why.
cards.problem: Find where results really differed and which causes could be fixed, keeping what the data showed separate from guesses about cause.

what_i_did.detail: Led share deep dives for Sydney, Christchurch and New Zealand, splitting movements by customer segment, membership, category and competitor activity.
Built a de-duplicated view of category users that explained to senior leaders why category growth and Uber Eats growth diverged.
Set up brand-level checks using the same measures and periods for every brand, including a switching analysis of a national restaurant chain's exclusive delivery deal.

what_i_did.summary: Hand findings to the right owner
what_i_did.detail: Passed local follow-ups to the teams with context, and contributed analysis to a New Zealand share response led by the New Zealand strategy lead.

cards.artifacts: Diagnostic decks, analysis workbooks, brand briefs, market briefs and prioritisation notes.
cards.outcome: The Sydney diagnosis moved the city from 'monitor' to 'act': Consumer launched targeted $0 delivery-fee offers, quests and promotions for new, low-frequency and lapsed customers in July 2025, followed by a targeted delivery-fee test.
cards.learning: Good diagnosis depends on the right level of detail: broad enough to see shared patterns, specific enough to find the cause you can actually act on.

cards.title: Building the APAC consumer dashboard end to end with AI
cards.headline: Built a single consumer dashboard for five APAC markets end to end with AI-assisted coding: about 108 governed metrics, daily refresh and AI-drafted weekly commentary, live within about four weeks of plan.
cards.trigger: Global and market reports didn't give one comparable regional view of consumers, so performance discussions started from different numbers.
cards.problem: The dashboard had to be trusted. Every metric had to tie back to finance and business-review definitions, refresh reliably, and be maintainable by one person.

what_i_did.detail: Wrote about 19 governed SQL queries (Presto/Hive, window functions, grouping sets, chunked backfills) covering active eaters, trips per user, lifecycle, membership, promotions and finance, all reviewed through pull requests.
Built the app, daily job and validation checks with Claude Code as a pair. It went from mock-up to live on real data in about four weeks, followed by about 120 pull requests of improvements.

Checked numbers against finance tables, the business-review sheets and a peer team's metric catalogue, fixed our own queries, and flagged upstream issues to their owners until settled months tied to finance reporting.
Added an AI-drafted weekly commentary section at the regional operations head's request, with a human check before it's shared.

cards.artifacts: Live dashboard, governed query library, validation checks, metric definitions and weekly commentary.
cards.outcome: Launched to 21 regional leaders and market leads, with 20 users in the first five weeks and 70% coming back. Its cohort data fed the regional capital-allocation review. It aims to be the business-review reference, but no forum is confirmed to run on it yet.
cards.learning: With AI as a pair, one person can build and maintain production-grade analytics, but only if every number is reconciled to a second source before anyone sees it.

cards.title: Rebuilding the ANZ market-intelligence report and tracking
cards.headline: Rebuilt and ran the monthly ANZ market-intelligence report for about 2.5 years as a single source of truth for leadership, and created a margin-of-error rule the global strategy team adopted.
cards.trigger: Market news and competitive data came from many places, and leaders needed one dependable monthly picture instead of scattered updates.
cards.problem: The report had to stay short and comparable month to month, avoid over-reacting to noisy share data, and keep running when people moved on.

what_i_did.detail: Rebuilt the monthly report around a fixed set of measures (category share, app downloads, fees, restaurant selection, satisfaction, brand spend, reliability and offers), with an analyst refreshing the data by script and me writing the commentary.
Created a margin-of-error rule: act on a share change only when it exceeds the error band and persists for two periods.

what_i_did.summary: Keep a memory of the market
what_i_did.detail: Ran a weekly promotions tracker and regular review meetings, and wrote data definitions and source notes so trackers didn't depend on anyone's memory.
Published to the ANZ leadership team and senior leads across departments around the same date each month, then handed the report over with a written guide.

cards.artifacts: Monthly reports and decks, weekly promotions tracker, data dictionaries, review notes, handover guide.
cards.outcome: The report ran monthly for about 2.5 years and informed consumer fee changes, supply-versus-demand investment in Sydney and Melbourne, and a buy-now-pay-later payment launch. The margin-of-error rule was written into the global strategy team's guidelines for reading share data, and my competitor-response framework was picked up by other markets.
cards.learning: Regular reports help decisions when they answer the same key questions each time and say how confident they are. A clear rule for what counts as a real change prevents a lot of wasted reaction.

cards.title: Setting up the APAC Consumer Strategy role
cards.headline: Defined a new regional consumer strategy role from scratch (scope, decision rights, mission, three pillars and key results) and saw it adopted in the regional consumer plan.
cards.trigger: After a September 2026 reorganisation I stepped into a newly created regional consumer strategy role, the first of its kind for the APAC team.
cards.problem: The role was deliberately broad. It had to be clear where the regional team coordinates, where it provides tools and methods, and where pricing, membership, market and product teams stay in charge.

what_i_did.detail: Compared how similar roles worked in the global, US and Canada, EMEA, Latin America and ANZ teams before drafting a scope proposal.

Wrote what the role would and wouldn't own, using a decision-rights framework, with input rights on fees and membership pricing and partners in consumer, pricing, marketplace, membership and strategy teams.
Drafted the mission, three pillars and key results (monthly active eaters and trips per user) with my manager, plus a step-by-step plan to consult and build.

cards.artifacts: Role scope proposal, decision-rights outline, mission and pillars, key results and a consult-and-build plan.
cards.outcome: The role, its mission and three pillars were adopted in the regional consumer plan, and I'm named the regional driver for the consumer dashboard and consumer home page work.
cards.learning: Agree who decides and how metrics are defined before investing in the build. A coordination role earns its place by giving teams tools, not by taking decisions from them.

cards.title: Responding proportionately to McDonald's $0.99 delivery promotion
cards.headline: Co-wrote the response to McDonald's $0.99 delivery promotion in Australia: segmented exposed customers, recommended a targeted membership trial over a broad fee cut, and set trigger-based monitoring.
cards.trigger: McDonald's launched a $0.99 delivery fee on its own channel in 2026, and leaders wanted to know how exposed Uber Eats customers were and how hard to respond.
cards.problem: Tell real competitive pressure apart from normal ups and downs, and avoid an expensive broad response that the evidence didn't justify.

what_i_did.detail: Segmented customers by membership, McDonald's loyalty and Uber Eats order frequency to find which groups were most at risk.
Recommended a 6-month Uber One trial for high-loyalty, high-frequency non-members rather than a broad $0 delivery fee.
Built monitoring with control and placebo groups, and held the broad fee cut behind a clear trigger instead of launching it pre-emptively.
Co-wrote the response deck for the country GM with the McDonald's account team.

cards.artifacts: Customer segmentation, scenario model, monitoring plan with triggers, leadership deck.
cards.outcome: The targeted trial went live, the trigger-based monitoring ran as designed, and the broad fee cut was never needed.
cards.learning: A credible response doesn't have to be immediate or broad. Uptake of the trial came in far below the full-uptake assumption in my cost model, so I now model opt-in explicitly.

cards.title: Consolidating regional membership priorities for annual planning
cards.headline: Consolidated 8 market membership requests into 7 regional product asks across 5 APAC markets for annual planning; 4 of the 7 were funded or part-funded in the following year's product plan.
cards.trigger: As regional membership product champion, I had to bring market requests, product dependencies and planning deadlines into one view before the regional leadership planning deadline.
cards.problem: Markets described their needs in different levels of detail and with different assumptions about timing, ownership and evidence. The roadmap had to show what was committed, blocked or only proposed without looking more settled than it was.

what_i_did.summary: Put every ask in one format
what_i_did.detail: Collected requests from Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan and Sri Lanka in a common format (customer problem, decision needed, dependencies, maturity, owner) and merged 8 market asks into 7 regional asks.
Wrote the regional membership priorities memo for leadership planning, backed by about ten research pages, and filed the planning intake and benefit-change timeline.

Supported a recurring product and operations sync built around decisions, dependencies and launches, with pre-reads, named owners and a decision log; recorded open disagreements instead of forcing consensus.

cards.artifacts: Regional priorities memo, market ask register, planning intake, benefit-change timeline and decision log.
cards.outcome: At the product funding review, 4 of the 7 regional asks were funded or part-funded in the following year's product plan. I held the regional view until membership moved to a separate team in the September reorganisation and handed it over.
cards.learning: Alignment doesn't mean agreeing on everything. It means being clear on what's known, what's disputed and who decides next, and showing uncertainty openly rather than hiding it in a polished list.

cards.title: Modelling the economics of a tiered membership and member benefits
cards.headline: Led the regional workstream on a tiered-membership concept for an APAC market and built the budget simulator myself with AI; it became the working budget tool in weekly cross-functional reviews, though the concept was not launched.
cards.trigger: A globally designed member-reward and tier idea needed adapting to an APAC market where members behave differently and the economics differ, and new benefits had to be paid for without simply adding cost.
cards.problem: Borrowed settings from another market wouldn't hold. A per-order benefit risked concentrating cost on already-loyal heavy users, and the design had to stay workable if the full product experience slipped.

what_i_did.detail: Built an interactive budget simulator with AI-assisted coding (React/TypeScript, 15 versions with automated checks) on real local trip data, with member groups, qualifying thresholds and expected usage instead of borrowed assumptions.

Showed where cost concentrates and laid out the product options: caps, delayed eligibility, minimum order conditions, and funding new benefits by reallocating existing member discount spend rather than adding to it.
Built a membership economics dashboard covering five markets from finance data, and showed gaps between data sources rather than forcing one answer.

Ran the weekly regional sync with product operations, the global membership team and the market team, and wrote the executive briefing on launch dependencies, legal requirements and a fallback using existing tools.

cards.artifacts: Budget simulator, membership economics dashboard, cost-sensitivity tables, assumptions list and an executive launch briefing.
cards.outcome: The simulator became the working budget tool in the weekly cross-functional reviews, and the cost-control options were costed side by side for the decision. The concept was not launched.
cards.learning: Reusing an idea across markets means reusing the modelling approach, not the numbers. A design that's cost-neutral on paper still needs a funding owner before it's real.

cards.title: Battery-swapping market entry strategy in India for a Japan-based multinational
cards.headline: Built the India market-entry strategy for a Japan-based multinational's EV battery-swapping business, from consumer surveys in 10+ cities to an entry plan for 40+ cities and partnership talks with 50+ firms.
cards.trigger: A Japan-based multinational wanted to know whether battery-as-a-service (riders swap or subscribe to batteries instead of buying them) could become a real business in India.
cards.problem: The strategy had to tie together demand, customer needs, pricing, operations and partners. A single adoption forecast wasn't enough, and the model hadn't been proven at scale in India.

what_i_did.detail: Ran consumer research with surveys across 10+ cities, and built market, feasibility and profitability models by customer segment.
Compared business-model assumptions and turned them into decisions on target customers, pricing, sales strategy and a phased entry plan covering 40+ cities.
Facilitated partnership discussions with CXOs of 50+ leading private and public-sector firms to secure the partners the model depended on.
Led a two-tier team of consultants through the research, modelling and recommendation work.

cards.artifacts: Market and city models, survey findings, commercial scenarios, a phased entry plan and a partner pipeline.
cards.outcome: Delivered the entry strategy and city roll-out plan, which led into a multi-stakeholder pilot (C51) that enabled the client's launch. The client's projected revenue from the business: <redacted>.
cards.learning: Test business-model assumptions against how things actually run. A promising technology needs a clear customer use and a believable path to repeat revenue.

cards.title: Adopting hexagon-based area clusters as ANZ's planning layer
cards.headline: Led ANZ's adoption of the global team's hexagon-based area clusters, the first international market to do so, and built the rules-based layer that tagged every area for targeting and planning.
cards.trigger: City-level planning was too coarse, and the global team had built an algorithm that grouped small hexagons into delivery areas.
cards.problem: The algorithm was global. ANZ needed it adopted quickly, made understandable to local teams, and linked to how they define and compare areas.

what_i_did.detail: Ran ANZ's feedback round and rollout with the global strategy team, regional operations and local operations; it went live in July 2025.
Built a rules-based grouping on top, comparing reliability, merchant coverage and share against medians, and refreshed it each quarter as governed tables.
Tagged every Australia and New Zealand area with a strategic posture, from 'build the experience' to 'defend share'.
Explained the logic in plain terms to strategy and operations colleagues.

cards.artifacts: Method document, tactical grouping tables, explainer deck, progress updates.
cards.outcome: The clusters became ANZ's base geographic layer, used to select priority areas, set sales territories, target delivery-fee offers and run the regional growth tracker, across Acquisition, Marketplace, Consumer and performance marketing. The global team built the clustering algorithm, not me.
cards.learning: Adopting a global method fast needs a local translation layer and plain explanations, not just the algorithm.

cards.title: Building ANZ's city strategy dashboards and tracker
cards.headline: Designed and maintained ANZ's city and area performance dashboards, which became the single source of truth for a seven-function growth working group and the monthly business review.
cards.trigger: Broad market strategy didn't give teams the local evidence they needed for city-level choices, or a shared base to revisit them.
cards.problem: Teams needed one trusted city and area view, with definitions everyone accepted and numbers that matched reference data.

what_i_did.detail: Designed the city and area tracker, monthly category-share dashboards and priority-city views, and specified every metric.
Built the Google Sheets layer myself while offshore analysts wrote and refreshed the SQL.
Checked analyst outputs against reference data and fixed definition errors before numbers reached leaders.
Fed priority-city data into the fortnightly working group and the monthly business review.

cards.artifacts: Dashboards, city and area tracker, maps, metric definitions, planning decks.
cards.outcome: In April 2026 the working group agreed all teams would work from this tracker as the single source of truth. My successor carried it into the second half of 2026, and the priority-city mapping moved to a governed data table.
cards.learning: A dashboard earns trust through reconciled numbers and stable definitions, not through more charts.

cards.title: Bringing AI into market-intelligence reporting
cards.headline: Led my team's early use of generative AI in ANZ market reporting: scripted the monthly report refresh, began automating category-share reporting with Claude Code, and set the metric definitions for an AI analyst bot.
cards.trigger: Reporting took analyst and strategist time every week, and generative AI tools were becoming good enough to help.
cards.problem: Tell apart the tasks AI could safely help with from the work that still needed context, checking and a person accountable for the final message.

what_i_did.detail: From October 2024, mapped the reporting steps and used ChatGPT, Gemini and NotebookLM for analysis and synthesis, keeping human review where findings were interpreted.
Refreshed the April 2026 market report by script in one task, and began automating the monthly category-share report with Claude Code over MCP.
Set the metric definitions for an AI analyst bot, built by the analytics team, that drafts weekly-review commentary. Its first output matched a teammate's manual report.
Wrote guidance on how I use AI for the regional operations team.

cards.artifacts: Workflow note, reporting template, bot metric definitions, AI guidance.
cards.outcome: A teammate and two to three analysts used the bot in weekly-review prep, and each new metric took about 3–4 hours to onboard. I didn't record hours saved.
cards.learning: General tool knowledge isn't proof that a workflow is ready. Pilot on one report, check it against the manual version, then widen.

cards.title: Diagnosing consumer pricing and promotion effectiveness across APAC
cards.headline: Led a set of hands-on pricing and promotion diagnostics across five APAC markets: what drives active eaters and frequency, whether fee changes hurt growth, and whether promo spend reaches the intended customers.
cards.trigger: Regional leadership asked what was holding back active eaters and trips per user, and whether fees and promotions were working as intended.
cards.problem: Fee and promo decisions are owned by pricing and market teams, so the work had to inform them without duplicating their analyses. Pricing effects are also confounded by the wider economy and overlapping changes.

what_i_did.detail: Analysed 24 months of monthly active eaters and trips per user across five markets, broken down by customer cohort and membership, and turned it into a 37-slide executive brief.
Reviewed the effect of fee changes and member fee benefits in two markets using same-customer panels, reconciled to the consumer dashboard (22-slide review).
Compared where fee and promotion spend actually goes by customer cohort against the global strategy's intent, and built a start-of-month promotion spend workbook for regional leadership.
Built a margin-neutral lever simulator for one market and a cohort-level fee and promotion plan (10 cohorts, 15 months, interactive explorer) for market teams to react to.

cards.artifacts: Executive briefs, a pricing-impact review, a lever simulator, a cohort plan explorer and a promotion spend workbook.
cards.outcome: In progress: the analyses feed the market teams' monthly pricing and promotion reviews and next year's plans, but no pricing decision is traced to them yet.
cards.learning: In a coordination role, the fastest path to impact is pre-wiring the decision owners and filling their gaps, not publishing a parallel answer.

cards.title: An executive-ready analysis playbook and AI deck-quality guide
cards.headline: Wrote a playbook for turning exploratory analysis into executive documents with AI (12 rules, an 8-step process, a starter kit, a reusable Claude skill and a 12-check quality gate), now used across my own executive work.
cards.trigger: A colleague asked how to get better executive-quality output from Claude, and my own analyses needed a repeatable way to go from exploration to a clear executive story.
cards.problem: AI makes it easy to produce lots of slides quickly. The hard part is one message per slide, figures that trace back to a source, and the right depth for each reader.

what_i_did.detail: Published an AI deck-quality guide with chart and slide rules, a colour palette and reusable chart-style code.
Turned the method behind a 37-slide executive brief into a playbook: 12 rules, an 8-step process, a starter kit and a reusable Claude skill.
Added a 12-check quality gate, including tracing every figure to its source and writing at 30-second, 3-minute and 30-minute depths.

cards.artifacts: AI deck-quality guide, executive-ready playbook, starter kit, reusable Claude skill and a quality checklist.
cards.outcome: I've applied it to my executive briefs, the quarterly newsletter, the cohort plan and a 44-slide deck where all 178 figures traced to a source. The colleague who asked rated both highly, but wider team adoption isn't proven yet.
cards.learning: AI speeds up the drafting; the value is in the rules that make the output trustworthy and easy for executives to read.

cards.title: Writing the business-trends story for the ANZ leadership planning offsite
cards.headline: Wrote the business-trends deep dive for the ANZ leadership planning offsite in May 2026 (17 slides, a 60-minute session for the country GM and direct reports), framing the second-half priorities.
cards.trigger: The ANZ leadership team needed a shared read of the business before setting second-half priorities at its planning offsite.
cards.problem: Avoid two traps: a pile of disconnected updates, or a big-picture story that couldn't be traced back to evidence.

what_i_did.detail: Structured the first-half story by consumer, marketplace, merchant and finance lens rather than by data source.
Added competitor moves, McDonald's $0.99 promotion, global trends and the macro picture.
Ended with second-half scenarios written to start a discussion, and flagged where evidence didn't support a firm conclusion.
Maintained the annual insights packs behind earlier leadership planning offsites.

cards.artifacts: Offsite deck, annual insights packs, research notes.
cards.outcome: The offsite set the ANZ second-half direction and priorities, and the deck was the shared fact base for that discussion. Its direct link to each choice isn't documented.
cards.learning: Executive narratives work when each section can be traced to evidence and is honest about where the evidence runs out.

cards.title: Running the consumer satisfaction program and rationalising research vendors
cards.headline: Ran the monthly ANZ consumer satisfaction survey, then rationalised the research vendors: ended two contracts and cut another's cost by about two-thirds while keeping the data teams relied on.
cards.trigger: Leadership wanted a consistent monthly read of consumer satisfaction, and the team was paying several research vendors for overlapping data.
cards.problem: A headline score on its own explains little, and a stock-take showed some of the data was noisy and not clearly used, costing about three hours a week to run.

what_i_did.detail: Owned the monthly satisfaction report from my first weeks: a general-population survey of about 2,000 respondents, monthly question updates, and commentary for the ANZ leadership team and senior leads.
Added pickup and New Zealand respondents, wrote an FAQ and definitions, and proposed linking the affordability goal to the fee-perception drivers in the survey.
After a stock-take, ended two survey contracts whose data was noisy or unused.
Renegotiated a data contract to about a third of its previous cost while keeping the delivery-time data teams depended on.

cards.artifacts: Monthly satisfaction reports, questionnaire and definitions, vendor stock-take, renegotiated contract.
cards.outcome: Annual research spend fell by <redacted>, with two contracts ended and one cut by about two-thirds, without losing data teams used. I found no evidence that a specific decision changed because of the survey itself.
cards.learning: Satisfaction programs work best when they stay consistent but are regularly asked to justify their cost. A stock-take of what is actually used is often the fastest way to save money.

cards.title: Data-driven marketing strategy to attract Indian travellers to Japan
cards.headline: Built a data-driven marketing strategy for a public-sector tourism organisation to attract Indian travellers to Japan, using 50,000+ customer records and 2,000+ interviews to set targeting, channels and media mix.
cards.trigger: A public-sector tourism organisation needed an approach built specifically for India to attract more travellers to Japan.
cards.problem: We had to work out which travellers were most promising, what appealed to them, and how they went from first hearing about Japan to planning a trip.

what_i_did.detail: Analysed 50,000+ customer records alongside consumer surveys to find the most promising traveller segments.
Drew on 2,000+ interviews plus travel-industry and expert input to map how each segment moves from awareness to booking.
Linked segments and journeys to content themes, media channels and a promotion plan.

cards.artifacts: A market study, traveller segment profiles, journey maps, content ideas and a marketing plan.
cards.outcome: Delivered the marketing policy (targeting, channels and media mix), grounded in segment evidence rather than general assumptions.
cards.learning: The key was linking evidence about the audience to a practical promotion plan, with local travel habits shaping the message and channel choices.

cards.title: Expansion and digital plan for a US utility-scale energy storage company
cards.headline: Built a phased business-expansion and digital-transformation plan for a US utility-scale energy storage company, prioritising functions, regions and products and scoping software to run grid-scale battery sites.
cards.trigger: A US-based utility-scale energy storage company wanted to expand and to use software to run its large battery sites better, getting more out of the storage and managing revenue.
cards.problem: Before deciding where to grow and what the software should do, the team had to connect business goals, day-to-day workflows, competitor offers and user needs.

what_i_did.detail: Used regional and competitor analysis to prioritise which functions, regions and products to expand first.
Interviewed stakeholders and mapped how storage sites are run day to day, from dispatch decisions to revenue management.
Benchmarked existing software and ranked the features that mattered most, setting the questions to answer before choosing a vendor or building.

what_i_did.summary: Phase the plan with the client
what_i_did.detail: Created a phased expansion plan together with the client's cross-functional team.

cards.artifacts: Regional and competitor analyses, process maps, feature lists, concept decks and a phased expansion plan.
cards.outcome: Delivered the phased expansion plan and software concept, which set the client's direction for development.
cards.learning: A good product idea starts with the decisions and workflows it supports. Feature lists mean more when the business process behind them is clear.

cards.title: Running an electric three-wheeler battery-swap pilot end to end
cards.headline: Ran a six-month battery-swap pilot for electric three-wheelers end to end, leading a five-person PMO across eight domestic and international partners; the pilot enabled the client's business launch.
cards.trigger: The battery-swapping entry strategy (C50) needed real-world proof. Vehicles, batteries, swap stations and daily operations had to work together on the road before the client committed to launch.
cards.problem: The pilot would only teach something useful if readiness, daily operations, problems and partner responsibilities were tracked in one place, across partners with different incentives.

what_i_did.detail: Set up and ran a five-person project management office covering timelines, resource plans, reporting and partner updates.
Kept eight domestic and international stakeholders across the vehicle, battery, station and operations workstreams aligned, with a named owner for every open issue.
Used kaizen and agile methods: regular operating reviews, one shared issue tracker, and fixes tested on the ground before the next review.
Organised the evidence into a clear view of what the pilot tested, what worked and what was still unresolved before scaling.

cards.artifacts: Pilot plan, operations and issue trackers, partner updates, operating-review decks and a final report.
cards.outcome: The pilot ran to completion and enabled the client's business launch. Pilot budget: <redacted>.
cards.learning: Pilots are as much about careful observation and fixing problems as about how the technology performs. Clear owners and a shared record make later scaling decisions credible.

cards.title: Feeding geo strategy into ANZ annual and half-year planning
cards.headline: Owned the ANZ geo plan and fed city-selection logic into annual and half-year planning; the regional growth program went into the 2026 plan as a named priority with its own goals.
cards.trigger: Planning cycles needed city and area choices that were evidence-based and linked to who would deliver them.
cards.problem: Plans came in at different levels of detail, and geo choices had to fit other teams' goals, headcount and budgets that I didn't own.

what_i_did.detail: Owned the geo plan and set the city-selection logic and city lists. Another teammate owned the overall ANZ plan document.
Fed city lists into Acquisition's 2026 plan, where Acquisition owned the goals and headcount and the country GM decided.
Pushed back on a New Zealand proposal covering far more areas than the evidence supported; it became a focused list of 12 cities.
Supplied priority-city data to the monthly and quarterly business reviews.

cards.artifacts: Geo plan, city lists, planning inputs, review data.
cards.outcome: The regional growth program went into the ANZ 2026 plan as a named priority with its own goals, and was one of five growth levers in an Australia growth-insights deck shared with the global team, with me as the named contact. I did not set budgets.
cards.learning: Planning input lands best when it's tied to a named owner's goals. Saying 'not this many' is as valuable as adding priorities.

cards.title: Coordinating which APAC markets join global membership features and tests
cards.headline: As the region's membership product point of contact, I took each global membership feature and test to five APAC markets with a recommendation and logged a clear yes or no from each.
cards.trigger: Global teams designed member features, benefits and reward challenges, and each APAC market needed a clear, evidence-based decision on whether to take part.
cards.problem: Markets differ in demand, commercial setup, regulation and ability to run tests that give clean answers, so one regional decision would have been wrong. Overlapping campaigns and late-loading audiences could also spoil comparison groups.

what_i_did.detail: Took each global test to the market leads in Australia and New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan and Sri Lanka with a recommendation based on country-level results, fit, cost tolerance and clashing changes, and logged each opt-in or opt-out. Product teams designed the tests.
Asked for clean control groups, first-exposure dates and clear rules for which campaign takes priority before results were read, and kept modelled estimates separate from real results.

Wrote product and measurement requirements for scaling partner-funded member offers (configuration, offer mapping, an incrementality standard) and backed the request for standard campaign spend tracking.
Built a demand and capacity forecast for student-membership eligibility checks, with growth and decline scenarios, and managed capacity top-ups until handover.

cards.artifacts: Market-fit tables, opt-in decision log, partner-offer requirements, a verification capacity tracker and forecast.
cards.outcome: Every global test in the period had a recorded decision from each of the five markets, made on local evidence rather than a blanket regional call. The tracking tools that later shipped were built by product teams, not me.
cards.learning: A cheap test isn't automatically useful, and a local win doesn't prove something works across a whole market. Decide the reading rules before the test starts.

cards.title: Bringing a global member-retention test to APAC markets
cards.headline: Carried a global cancellation-offer test into Japan, Taiwan and Sri Lanka and set the rule that an opt-out isn't churn until renewal cohorts mature; all three markets were recommended to keep the winning offer.
cards.trigger: Retention was a top priority in mid-2026, and members who signalled they'd cancel needed a better response than one standard discount.
cards.problem: One rescue offer hides real differences between plan types and preferences, and results can't be trusted until the setup is proven and there's a valid control group. The test itself was designed and run by global product teams.

what_i_did.detail: Shared the interim read with the regional team and asked the Taiwan and Sri Lanka teams to opt in to the global cancellation-offer test, alongside Japan.
Kept members who said they'd cancel separate from members who actually left, and insisted opt-outs weren't counted as churn until renewal-aligned cohorts had matured.
Measured win-back among opt-outs after the Taiwan price change (<redacted>), labelled it observational because there was no control group, and checked approved designs against what was really live.

cards.artifacts: Interim read-out, market opt-in requests, measurement notes in the price-change memo.
cards.outcome: The global read-out recommended keeping the winning cancellation offer in all three markets I brought in (lift: <redacted>). I can't claim my nudge drove those market decisions.
cards.learning: Prove the setup is complete and the control group is valid before claiming members were won back, and define precisely who qualifies for a win-back offer.

cards.title: Reviewing membership sign-up offers: trial length and annual plans
cards.headline: Contributed the analysis behind a review of extended free trials in one market and a five-market evidence pack on annual plans, recommending offers by customer history rather than one blanket cap.
cards.trigger: Sign-up offers needed to be judged on how many people became paying members, not just how many signed up.
cards.problem: Longer free access boosts sign-ups but delays finding out who will pay, and promotion-driven demand had to be separated from demand for the plan itself. The offer decisions sat with the market and global membership teams.

what_i_did.detail: Recommended against a blanket cap on trial length: remove the longest trials from the least-retentive never-member and inactive cohorts, use short trials for lapsed paying members, and test a short trial followed by discounted months.
Compared what was live with what was intended and flagged out-of-date long-trial campaigns that were still running.
Built a five-market evidence pack on plan mix, continuation, engagement and pre-sign-up frequency, recommending monthly as the entry plan with an upgrade offer once members had seen value.

cards.artifacts: Trial-length review, five-market annual-plan evidence pack, decision tables by customer group.
cards.outcome: The out-of-date long-trial campaigns I flagged were later switched off, and the market owner shortened the longest trials for low-frequency segments. Those decisions were theirs, and I can't trace them directly to my work.
cards.learning: Agree the main goal before tuning how long an offer lasts. Total members, paying members and long-term value can point to different answers at the same time.

cards.title: Consumer inputs to regional planning, capital allocation and geo strategy
cards.headline: Supplied the consumer analysis for three regional planning processes: a stress test of a market's annual plan, customer lifetime-value inputs for capital allocation, and consumer-lever principles for next year's geo strategy.
cards.trigger: Regional planning, capital allocation and the geo strategy each needed a consumer view, and the owners asked for analyst input.
cards.problem: I didn't own any of these plans, so the inputs had to be easy to use and clearly separated from the owners' decisions. Gross cohort data also overstates the value of promotion-driven customers unless cannibalisation is accounted for.

what_i_did.detail: Cross-checked a market's annual plan against dashboard data before plan lock, flagging the growth, promotion-efficiency and funding assumptions worth pressure-testing.
Produced lifetime-value inputs for first-time and returning eaters for the regional capital-allocation review, with an explicit cannibalisation adjustment against a break-even threshold.

Wrote a one-page consumer point of view for the regional geo strategy: weight a promotion by area only when its return depends on the place, not the eater, and separate productised levers from manual ones.

cards.artifacts: Plan cross-check page, lifetime-value inputs, consumer-lever principles and a lever sheet.
cards.outcome: In progress: the lifetime-value inputs were used in the capital-allocation review, and the geo-strategy owner and I agreed I'd hand over a lever sheet for next year's campaigns. No plan figure has changed because of my cross-check so far.
cards.learning: An analyst input lands best when it's framed in the owner's structure and flags risks without second-guessing their call.

cards.title: Prioritising work for an offshore analytics team
cards.headline: Set priorities for offshore analysts supporting ANZ strategy through a visible request queue; the market report turned around in one day, and I mentored three junior teammates.
cards.trigger: Business questions often got lost on the way to becoming analysis, because context and priorities had to cross team and time-zone boundaries.
cards.problem: I didn't line-manage the analysts, so I had to make priorities clear and useful enough that the work moved anyway.

what_i_did.detail: Ran a twice-weekly sync with two to three analysts and a teammate, with one visible request queue covering the market report, dashboards, weekly review and an analyst bot.

what_i_did.summary: Tie each ask to a decision
what_i_did.detail: Agreed for each request which decision it supported, and separated urgent questions from foundational work.
Caught a duplicate-area error that inflated regional numbers and had it fixed, and onboarded a new supply metric.
Mentored three junior teammates on dashboards and analysis, and handed weekly-review ownership to one of them.

cards.artifacts: Priority tracker, request brief template, meeting format, handover notes.
cards.outcome: The April 2026 market report turned around in one day, and weekly-review ownership moved to a teammate in April 2026. Gains in speed and quality are self-reported; they weren't measured.
cards.learning: Influence without line authority comes from making priorities clear and every request easy to act on.

cards.title: Case study of a competitor's market entry
cards.headline: Contributed to a structured case study of a competitor's market entry, separating market-specific details from lessons reusable in other markets.
cards.trigger: A competitor's entry into a market was a chance to study how positioning and market conditions interact.
cards.problem: Go beyond a timeline of events and find lessons for other markets without overstating cause and effect.

what_i_did.detail: Organised it around context, visible moves, how others responded and alternative explanations.
Compared the phases of the entry and wrote down what was uncertain.
Split details specific to this market from questions reusable in future reviews.

cards.artifacts: Case-study deck, research notes, comparison tables, discussion guide.
cards.outcome: The team got a reusable way to study market entries and ask better questions before applying lessons elsewhere.
cards.learning: Strong case studies keep the context rather than reducing events to a simple success or failure story.

cards.title: Screening equity investments in beverages
cards.headline: Screened India's beverage market for a Japanese beverage company considering an equity investment: shortlisted targets, supported early conversations and commercial due diligence, and built the valuation model.
cards.trigger: A Japanese beverage company was considering investing in an Indian company.
cards.problem: The decision depended on category demand, competition, how well each target fitted, and valuation assumptions.

what_i_did.detail: Analysed the market and customers to see where demand and competition were heading.
Screened and shortlisted possible investment targets against fit criteria.
Supported early conversations and commercial due diligence with shortlisted targets.
Built the valuation model and scenarios, with assumptions spelled out.

cards.artifacts: A market screen, a target shortlist, due-diligence notes and valuation scenarios.
cards.outcome: Delivered the market screen, shortlist and valuation scenarios that framed the client's investment discussions.
cards.learning: Spell out the investment case and valuation assumptions before narrowing down to one target.

cards.title: Integration planning after an FMCG acquisition
cards.headline: Planned the post-acquisition integration of two FMCG businesses in India with business leaders and specialists: simplified overlapping processes, designed the new organisation and set milestones and success measures.
cards.trigger: After a cross-border acquisition, two consumer-goods businesses needed to combine their operations and teams.
cards.problem: The plan had to deal with overlapping processes, who would own what, milestones, and legal and tax requirements.

what_i_did.detail: Mapped both companies' processes and worked with business leaders to simplify where they overlapped.
Supported the organisation workstream with the new structure and ownership of each process.
Planned milestones and success measures, working with legal and tax specialists on their requirements.

cards.artifacts: An integration plan, milestones and success measures, and organisation-workstream materials.
cards.outcome: Delivered the integration plan with milestones, success measures and the organisation design.
cards.learning: Integration needs named owners and a clear order of decisions, not just a savings target.

cards.title: Benchmarking against public company results
cards.headline: Ran regular benchmarking of comparable companies' public results for ANZ leadership, separating comparable trends from metrics that only looked alike.
cards.trigger: Comparable businesses published regular results, a useful but scattered view of how they were changing.
cards.problem: Different companies define their public numbers differently, so comparisons had to be careful not to treat unlike metrics as the same.

what_i_did.detail: Checked source quality, definitions and time periods before comparing anything.
Compared broad trends and wrote down where comparisons held and where they broke down.
Turned technical disclosures into short takeaways for internal discussion.

cards.artifacts: Benchmarking notes, comparison tables, leadership summaries.
cards.outcome: The team got a repeatable, careful way to discuss comparable businesses' public results alongside the monthly market report.
cards.learning: The most useful benchmark is often not a ranking but a clear view of where comparisons hold and where they break down.

cards.title: Digitising freight management for a global manufacturer
cards.headline: Helped a global manufacturer standardise freight management across its hubs: prioritised system requirements, ran the vendor comparison and planned the process and change-management steps for each team.
cards.trigger: A global manufacturer wanted its hubs to manage freight the same way on one system.
cards.problem: Bidding, booking, tracking, vendor choice and adoption were linked. Treating them as separate technology tasks wouldn't work.

what_i_did.detail: Helped decide which system features mattered most across hubs with different ways of working.
Set up the vendor comparison against agreed criteria.
Worked out the process and change-management steps each team needed, plus performance measures to track adoption.

cards.artifacts: Requirements, vendor comparisons, an implementation plan and performance measures.
cards.outcome: Delivered the requirements, vendor comparison and implementation plan, with measures to track adoption across hubs.
cards.learning: A new system only pays off when the way people work changes too. Picking the right product is not enough.

cards.title: Go-to-market strategy for a data-centre solution
cards.headline: Contributed to the go-to-market strategy for a technology group's all-in-one data-centre offer in India: competitor, product and customer research shaped the offer, target customers and sales approach.
cards.trigger: A technology group explored offering an all-in-one data-centre solution in India.
cards.problem: Several product and service lines had to be packaged into one offer built around what customers needed.

what_i_did.detail: Contributed to competitor and product benchmarking.
Helped plan and run customer research on what buyers needed from a single provider.
Helped define the offer, the target customers and how to sell it.

cards.artifacts: Benchmarking, a customer-research plan, market positioning and go-to-market materials.
cards.outcome: Delivered the positioning and go-to-market materials; the work led into the related organisation redesign (C67).
cards.learning: A service offer has to start from the customer's problem and how it will be delivered, not from bundling existing products.

cards.title: Comparing competitor research across APAC markets
cards.headline: Built a side-by-side view of competitor research across five APAC markets, showing what existed, how reliable and recent it was, and what to improve first.
cards.trigger: I wanted to know how well competitor research could support consumer and membership decisions in each market across the region.
cards.problem: Markets had different research sources, definitions, update frequencies and quality. Missing information couldn't be treated as proof that nothing existed.

what_i_did.detail: Defined a shared list of research types and put every market's inputs into the same format.
Separated what was confirmed from what was only reported or unclear, and noted how fresh and reliable each source was instead of giving a single rating.
Grouped related items and built a view of which gaps to close first, keeping local detail visible while making the comparison easy to scan.

cards.artifacts: Cross-market comparison table, source quality list, shared categories and a priority list.
cards.outcome: Regional and market teams had one shared starting point for discussing research gaps and where to invest.
cards.learning: A useful maturity view shows how good and how recent the evidence is, not just a score.

cards.title: Measuring consumer affordability
cards.headline: Designed a transparent way to measure what customers actually pay across order types, splitting price into its parts so teams could debate affordability on evidence.
cards.trigger: Teams needed a clearer way to talk about what customers actually pay across different kinds of orders.
cards.problem: Affordability isn't one displayed price. It depends on what people order, fees, promotions and what they compare against, and all of these change.

what_i_did.detail: Defined a measure that splits the price experience into menu price, fees and promotions.
Checked whether comparisons still made sense across periods and situations.
Explained the assumptions in plain language so people could question them instead of treating the index as a black box.

cards.artifacts: Measurement model, method explainers, research notes, review summaries.
cards.outcome: The team got a reusable, transparent way to discuss consumer value, which fed the satisfaction program and leadership planning discussions.
cards.learning: Affordability measures are more useful when their assumptions are visible and they can answer several different questions.

cards.title: Reading fuel-cost signals for consumer behaviour
cards.headline: Contributed a note turning rising fuel prices into testable hypotheses about consumer behaviour across rides and delivery, with alternative explanations built in.
cards.trigger: Fuel prices were changing, and people asked how consumers might change their behaviour across rides and delivery.
cards.problem: It was tempting to read cause into coincidence, so the news had to become careful questions instead.

what_i_did.detail: Reviewed the fuel-price trend and listed the ways consumers might plausibly respond.
Separated what we could observe right away from what needed deeper checking.
Treated other explanations as part of the analysis and kept the questions testable against our own data.

cards.artifacts: Research note and fuel-price signal tracker.
cards.outcome: Leaders got a structured set of questions to test, instead of a headline assumption.
cards.learning: Big economic trends are good prompts but weak conclusions. Spell out the mechanism, list other explanations and decide what evidence would change your mind.

cards.title: Assessing buy now, pay later for food delivery
cards.headline: Contributed a research note on how buy now, pay later could fit food delivery, framing what would need to be true for customers, operations and the experience.
cards.trigger: Buy now, pay later was growing in retail, and the team wanted to know whether it belonged in food delivery.
cards.problem: Separate a broad payments trend from the questions that matter for on-demand delivery: would customers care, how would it work operationally, and what might it cost the experience.

what_i_did.detail: Broke the topic into testable questions on customer interest, operational fit and cost to the experience.
Reviewed available material without treating take-up elsewhere as proof it would work here.
Summarised the findings in a short strategic note that listed the biggest open gaps for later work.

cards.artifacts: Research note and working model.
cards.outcome: The note fed discussion ahead of a buy-now-pay-later payment option launching in ANZ.
cards.learning: Assessing an adjacent area is most useful when it spells out what would need to be true, rather than rushing to a recommendation.

cards.title: Analysing membership coverage across ANZ
cards.headline: Built a structured member versus non-member comparison across ANZ that separated availability, relevance and engagement gaps, turning membership coverage into a regular strategy input.
cards.trigger: I wanted to understand where membership was strong across the ANZ customer experience and where our picture had gaps.
cards.problem: Compare members and non-members consistently without boiling it down to one number, and separate overall coverage from differences driven by location, restaurant choice or behaviour.

what_i_did.detail: Built a structured member versus non-member comparison and checked how it changed across markets and situations.
Treated availability, relevance and engagement as separate problems, each with a different owner.
Wrote decision questions for the teams that could act, and kept sensitive performance detail out of wide circulation.

cards.artifacts: Analysis pack, diagnostic framework, decision brief.
cards.outcome: Membership coverage became a regular input to strategy instead of a one-off report.
cards.learning: Treating availability, relevance and engagement as separate problems makes each one solvable by a named team.

cards.title: Designing a business model for a connected-car service
cards.headline: Outlined customer offers, engagement mechanics and pricing options for a connected-car service, and tested each option through financial forecasts and scenario discussions to find a model built on repeat use.
cards.trigger: A car maker wanted its connected-car service to keep delivering value to customers and to support a workable business model.
cards.problem: The offer had to connect how often people would use it, how the service was designed and the financial assumptions. A list of features wouldn't guarantee people kept using it.

what_i_did.detail: Helped outline possible customer offers and ways to keep users engaged over time.
Set out alternative ways to charge for the service, from bundled to paid add-on models.
Tested what each option meant through financial forecasts and scenario discussions, with usage and revenue assumptions looked at together.

cards.artifacts: Business-model options, engagement ideas, financial forecasts and strategy decks.
cards.outcome: Delivered business-model options with a forecast for each, so the client could compare monetisation paths on the same usage assumptions.
cards.learning: Revenue follows repeated customer value. Usage assumptions and revenue forecasts have to be built and challenged together.

cards.title: Screening renewable-energy investment opportunities
cards.headline: Screened renewable-energy markets and companies in India and other Asian markets for an energy investor, combining policy, economics and partner fit into a shortlist and supporting early conversations.
cards.trigger: An energy investor wanted to find promising renewable-energy opportunities in India and other Asian markets.
cards.problem: An attractive market wasn't enough. Policy, economics, possible partners and strategic fit all mattered.

what_i_did.detail: Researched market conditions, policy and technology options using a PEST-style framework.
Helped screen and shortlist companies against strategic-fit criteria.
Supported early conversations with shortlisted companies to check fit before deeper work.

cards.artifacts: Market screens, target lists, research reports and discussion materials.
cards.outcome: Delivered market screens and a target shortlist, and supported the investor's first conversations with shortlisted companies.
cards.learning: Use a broad market scan to decide what to investigate next, not as the final investment decision.

cards.title: Business plan for a two-wheeler finance arm
cards.headline: Contributed to the feasibility study and phased business plan for a two-wheeler maker's own finance arm, covering customer groups, loan products, partner structure and operations.
cards.trigger: A two-wheeler manufacturer looked at whether its own finance business could help customers buy and improve results.
cards.problem: The idea needed a viable customer group, loan terms, a partner structure and the ability to run it.

what_i_did.detail: Contributed customer and competitor analysis to find groups the finance arm could serve.
Worked through loan product and operating questions, including dealer processes and collections.
Contributed to a phased business plan with business-model options.

cards.artifacts: Feasibility reports, customer research, business-model options and implementation plans.
cards.outcome: Delivered the feasibility study and phased business plan.
cards.learning: A finance business has to balance customer value, risk, dealer operations and the ability to collect repayments.

cards.title: Cost-reduction programme for an automotive business
cards.headline: Benchmarked costs along the automotive value chain for an automotive business, identified where performance lagged, and helped plan a multi-part cost-reduction programme.
cards.trigger: An automotive business wanted to find lasting cost savings.
cards.problem: A believable programme needed comparisons across functions and a focus on initiatives that could actually be delivered.

what_i_did.detail: Benchmarked costs function by function along the value chain.
Identified where performance lagged and sized each opportunity.
Helped plan a cost-reduction roadmap with owners and timelines for each initiative.

cards.artifacts: A benchmark, a map of savings opportunities and a cost-reduction roadmap.
cards.outcome: Delivered the benchmark and a cost-reduction roadmap, with an owner, a timeline and practical limits set out for each opportunity.
cards.learning: A benchmark becomes useful when each opportunity has an owner, a timeline and a clear view of practical limits.

cards.title: Vehicle demand forecasting and supply-chain planning
cards.headline: Built a region- and product-level demand forecast for an automotive manufacturer, combining bottom-up and top-down methods, and set up a regular review process for supply and inventory planning.
cards.trigger: An automotive manufacturer needed a better basis for planning supply and inventory.
cards.problem: Demand varied by region and product features, so one broad forecast couldn't guide day-to-day decisions.

what_i_did.detail: Combined bottom-up and top-down forecasts so each could check the other.
Split the forecast by region and product features to match how supply decisions are made.
Set up a regular review process tying each model update to the supply or inventory decision it should improve.

cards.artifacts: A forecast model, regional and product breakdowns, inventory recommendations and a review schedule.
cards.outcome: Delivered the forecast model and a recurring review process for supply and inventory planning.
cards.learning: Make forecast assumptions visible and tie each model update to the decision it should improve.

cards.title: Research on electric vehicle policy and industry in India
cards.headline: Reviewed India's evolving EV regulation, infrastructure and industry incentives, and turned them into scenarios and decision questions for clients weighing electric-mobility investment and rollout.
cards.trigger: Clients needed to understand how policy and industry changes in India's electric mobility sector would affect their investment and rollout options.
cards.problem: Choices depended on a changing mix of regulation, infrastructure, incentives and the interests of different groups, and much of it was uncertain.

what_i_did.detail: Reviewed national and state regulations and incentive schemes as they changed.
Mapped the market and key stakeholders across vehicle makers, energy and government.
Framed findings as scenarios and questions for decision-makers where implementation or timing was unclear.

cards.artifacts: Policy notes, market studies, stakeholder maps and presentations.
cards.outcome: Delivered policy notes and scenario framings for clients' EV investment and rollout discussions.
cards.learning: Policy research is more valuable when it explains which practical choices it changes and is open about uncertainty in how policies will be carried out.

cards.title: Strategy for a blockchain-based mobility platform
cards.headline: Assessed whether a blockchain-based platform could let European mobility operators share data and settle transactions, mapping partners, regulation and business-model options.
cards.trigger: A mobility platform idea needed a way for different operators to share data and handle transactions with each other.
cards.problem: The strategy had to show where the technology actually solved a business problem, which partners were needed and how it could grow.

what_i_did.detail: Looked at the regulatory and technology questions to see where the platform solved a genuine coordination problem.
Mapped possible partners and what each would need to take part.
Compared platform and product options alongside the market and business model.

cards.artifacts: A feasibility assessment, a partner map, business-model options and a strategy deck.
cards.outcome: Delivered the feasibility assessment and business-model options for the client's go/no-go discussion.
cards.learning: Judge a new technology by the coordination problem it solves and whether partners actually want to take part.

cards.title: India–Japan trade and industry competitiveness analysis
cards.headline: Researched India's trade position and industry competitiveness for a Japanese public-sector client, linking trade patterns to sector barriers and policy options for India–Japan policy talks.
cards.trigger: A Japanese public-sector project needed evidence on India's trade position and how competitive its industries were.
cards.problem: The analysis had to connect big-picture trade patterns with barriers in specific sectors and realistic policy responses.

what_i_did.detail: Analysed trade flows and industry structure to find where India was competitive and where it lagged.
Compared policies and gathered stakeholder input to pin down sector-specific barriers.
Coordinated research inputs and prepared discussion points and recommendations for bilateral policy talks.

cards.artifacts: Trade and sector analysis, meeting decks, policy notes and symposium material.
cards.outcome: Delivered the analysis, policy notes and symposium material used in India–Japan policy discussions.
cards.learning: Separate what the data shows from what negotiations can realistically achieve. Work across governments also depends on careful coordination and giving proper credit.

cards.title: Making business-review reporting repeatable
cards.headline: Supplied priority-city data to the ANZ monthly business review, covered weekly reviews, and documented the reporting steps so the pack no longer depended on a few people.
cards.trigger: Regular business reviews needed a more repeatable path from raw updates to a clear story for leadership.
cards.problem: Putting the pack together was manual and repetitive, inputs were inconsistent, and the know-how sat with only a few people.

what_i_did.detail: Supplied the priority-city section of the ANZ monthly business review and covered the weekly review when needed.
Documented recurring steps, checks and story structure so someone else could produce the pack.
Standardised templates first, then looked for steps that could be automated.

cards.artifacts: Business-review sections, reporting template, process documentation, handover guide.
cards.outcome: Ownership of the weekly review passed cleanly to a teammate in April 2026 using the written process.
cards.learning: Automating reporting works best once the process is written down. Clear check points and notes on judgement calls matter as much as the mechanical steps.

cards.title: Running the restaurants and retail strategy meeting
cards.headline: Supported a regular restaurants and retail strategy meeting that linked weekly priorities to business reviews, with clear follow-up and a split between updates and decisions.
cards.trigger: Restaurants and retail work needed a regular meeting that linked weekly priorities to the wider business reviews.
cards.problem: Without it, topics were discussed in separate meetings, with no consistent link between immediate delivery questions and longer-term planning.

what_i_did.detail: Grouped updates and highlighted dependencies so the meeting focused on what needed deciding.
Kept an action tracker so open questions didn't get lost between meetings.
Adjusted the level of detail for each audience and time horizon.

cards.artifacts: Meeting format and schedule, business-review deck, action tracker.
cards.outcome: The meeting gave restaurants and retail work a consistent storyline into business reviews.
cards.learning: A useful regular meeting needs a consistent storyline, clear follow-up, and a clear split between sharing information, solving problems and making decisions.

cards.title: Editing the quarterly consumer newsletter for APAC
cards.headline: Wrote and edited the Q3 2026 APAC consumer newsletter, giving regional leadership and five market teams one view of consumer performance, including the lowlights, and the team's priorities.
cards.trigger: Regional leadership and market teams heard consumer updates through separate meetings at different levels of detail, and needed one quarterly view of what changed and what needed attention.
cards.problem: The update had to add to meetings rather than repeat them, cover five markets and five consumer workstreams, and stay honest about what wasn't going well.

what_i_did.detail: Served as chief editor with a contractor as associate editor: drafted and built the edition, took it through review with my manager, and sent it to seven distribution lists across leadership and the market teams.
Chose to report the lowlights alongside the wins, and linked the update to the new consumer charter and upcoming product asks.
Organised it around performance, decisions, progress and risks, used the same structure throughout, and checked uncertain items with their owners before sending.

cards.artifacts: Quarterly newsletter page and email, with a communications calendar.
cards.outcome: Leadership and market leads replied, and replies corrected one partner read-out claim and prompted a follow-up read-out. The newsletter is now a standing quarterly item on the team agenda. I found no decision it triggered directly.
cards.learning: A good internal update saves the reader interpretation work. Reporting the lowlights builds more trust than a highlights reel.

cards.title: Handing over my ANZ strategy and planning role
cards.headline: Handed over a broad ANZ strategy role through a written, workstream-by-workstream guide; the market report, weekly review and growth tracker all kept running under new owners.
cards.trigger: I was moving from ANZ strategy and planning to a regional consumer role and wanted to leave the work in good shape.
cards.problem: A list of open tasks wasn't enough. The new owners needed to know which decisions recurred, what stakeholders expected, which reports existed and which questions still needed judgement.

what_i_did.detail: Wrote down the purpose, timing and stakeholders of each workstream.
Separated finished work from open decisions, and listed every report and dashboard the team used.
Flagged dependencies, access needs and assumptions the new owners should verify rather than inherit.
Moved the weekly review and market report to a teammate in April–May 2026 before leaving.

cards.artifacts: Handover document, workstream list, dashboard list, transition checklist.
cards.outcome: The market report, weekly review and regional growth tracker kept running after I left, and the tracker was extended into the second half of 2026.
cards.learning: A good handover explains how decisions get made, not just where the files are.

cards.title: Choosing which Southeast Asian markets to enter for cosmetics
cards.headline: Compared Southeast Asian countries for a Japanese beauty group's expansion on growth, category trends and consumer needs, and helped shape a regional go-to-market plan.
cards.trigger: A diversified Japanese beauty group explored expanding in Southeast Asia.
cards.problem: Country choices had to reflect market growth, category trends and what consumers wanted, and whether one regional approach could work.

what_i_did.detail: Researched economic and cosmetics trends and compared priority countries on shared criteria.
Built a market model to compare opportunity across countries.
Helped shape a regional go-to-market plan that respected differences between countries.

cards.artifacts: Country screens, a market model, consumer insights and go-to-market recommendations.
cards.outcome: Delivered the country prioritisation and regional go-to-market recommendations.
cards.learning: A regional strategy needs shared criteria while still respecting differences between countries.

cards.title: Reusing and recycling EV batteries
cards.headline: Screened second-life uses for EV batteries for an automotive client, reviewing technical, customer and policy requirements and assessing potential recycling partners.
cards.trigger: An automotive client wanted to know how batteries could keep creating value after their life in a vehicle.
cards.problem: Possible reuses, technical requirements, policy and recycling options all had to be assessed together.

what_i_did.detail: Helped screen possible second-life uses for batteries.
Reviewed customer and policy requirements for each use.
Assessed potential recycling partners for end-of-life handling.

cards.artifacts: A map of reuse opportunities, policy analysis, a partner shortlist and research materials.
cards.outcome: Delivered the reuse-opportunity map and recycling-partner shortlist.
cards.learning: Separate how valuable a reuse idea is from what it takes to deploy it safely and handle batteries at end of life.

cards.title: Screening next-generation battery technologies
cards.headline: Assessed next-generation battery technologies for a trading company's R&D team against practical and commercial criteria, and built a ranking of which to investigate further.
cards.trigger: A trading company's R&D team wanted to find battery technologies that could become commercially useful.
cards.problem: The technologies differed in maturity, cost, use, demand and competition, so no single performance measure could rank them fairly.

what_i_did.detail: Defined practical and commercial criteria that worked across technologies at different stages.
Assessed each technology on maturity, cost, use cases, demand and competition.
Built a prioritisation matrix of which technologies to investigate further.

cards.artifacts: A technology landscape, evaluation criteria, a prioritisation matrix and a research deck.
cards.outcome: Delivered the technology landscape and a prioritised shortlist for the R&D team's next phase.
cards.learning: Spell out assumptions about maturity and commercial readiness when comparing technologies at different stages.

cards.title: Reorganising teams to deliver a data-centre offer
cards.headline: Helped design the operating model that let separate business units deliver one joined-up data-centre offer, with a transformation roadmap and a plan to bring stakeholders along.
cards.trigger: The new data-centre offer (C66) needed business units that had always sold separate products to work together.
cards.problem: One joined-up service needed clear responsibilities, incentives, sales processes and a step-by-step transition.

what_i_did.detail: Helped design how the future organisation would work, including ownership and incentives.
Compared how competitors organised similar offers.
Planned how to bring stakeholders along and manage the change in stages.

cards.artifacts: An organisation blueprint, a transformation roadmap, a stakeholder plan and an operating-model deck.
cards.outcome: Delivered the organisation blueprint and transformation roadmap.
cards.learning: A joined-up offer to customers depends on internal ownership and incentives that support it.

cards.title: Car buyer segments and pricing research
cards.headline: Ran qualitative and quantitative consumer studies for car makers, including interviews, surveys, in-home observation and pricing exercises, and turned them into segment profiles that guided model, pricing and marketing decisions.
cards.trigger: Car makers needed consumer evidence to support decisions on models, pricing and marketing.
